title: Sam and the training that faded

narration: Imagine Sam, a full day of new software training.
Sam nods along, takes notes, feels ready.
Everyone says it went well.
Sam leaves with a full notepad.
beats.visual_intent: Cartoon Sam at a desk with a laptop and a full notepad, smiling, a bright skill icon glowing on the desk.

grounding.claim: Sam and the training day are an illustrative scene

narration: A week later, Sam opens the software.
The cursor blinks.
Sam cannot remember where to start.
The notes are right there.
They do not help.
beats.visual_intent: Same desk, a week on: the notepad lies open but untouched, Sam frowns at a blank screen with a blinking cursor, the skill icon dull.

grounding.claim: Sam is stuck a week after training

narration: By the end, you will know what Sam could have done.
Say, ten minutes, spread over a few days.
Then the training is still there,
when the real task arrives.
And you can do the same for your next training.
beats.visual_intent: Presenter beside a small calendar where short ten-minute blocks appear on separate days, ahead of a task marker.

grounding.claim: Ten minutes is an illustrative amount of practice
Practice spread over several days usually lasts longer

narration: You have been Sam, haven't you?
You sat through good training.
Then the real task showed up, and half of it was gone.
So watch what happens to the learning.
beats.visual_intent: A sticky week calendar on Sam's desk; the training notes pinned on it blur a little from day to day.

grounding.claim: Viewer's own half-lost training is a shared experience
Learning fades when not revisited

narration: Look at the skill icon on Sam's desk.
Day one, it is bright.
Sam knows the steps.
Then the days pass, and nothing revisits it.
The icon starts to fade.
beats.visual_intent: The skill icon on Sam's desk starts bright and visibly dims, a faint fade line tracing its brightness against the days.

grounding.claim: Memory for new material fades when not revisited

narration: Notice where it drops fastest.
Right after the training.
Then the fading slows down.
Day by day, less is lost.
beats.visual_intent: The fade line drops steeply on the first days then flattens, labels sitting on the steep part and the flat part of the curve; the icon dims to match.

grounding.claim: Forgetting is fastest soon after learning and slows down

narration: That is the shape. Steep first, then gentle.
No exact figures here.
They vary with the person and the material.
So we keep to the shape.
beats.visual_intent: The curve held on screen with its axes left unmarked, no numbers on either axis, one small tag saying the rate varies.

grounding.claim: Rate varies by material, person and how well it was learned, so no figures

narration: And Sam did nothing after the training.
Nothing brought the skill back.
So whether it stuck was left to chance.
Fading is fastest early.
beats.visual_intent: Sam leaning back, hands off the keyboard, while the icon sits dim at the bottom of the curve; a coin hovers over the desk.

grounding.claim: One session with no follow-up leaves later remembering to chance
Fading is fastest early

narration: Now say Sam has ten minutes of practice.
Two ways to spend them.
All at once, today.
Or in short visits, on later days.
beats.visual_intent: Two timelines stacked, same total effort drawn as the same amount of colour: one thick block on day one, and several thin slices on later days.

grounding.claim: Ten minutes of practice is an illustrative amount
Same practice can be one block or spread over sessions

narration: Cram it into one block, and it feels great.
Sam is sharp tomorrow.
Good for a test soon after.
Cramming does work for that.
beats.visual_intent: On the one-block timeline the skill line shoots up after the block and stays high for the next day.

grounding.claim: Cramming can feel productive and can help for a test soon after

narration: But look past tomorrow.
After that block, it fades faster.
Nothing lifts it again.
beats.visual_intent: The one-block line slides down after its peak with no further lifts, the slope steeper than the other timeline.

grounding.claim: Cramming tends to fade faster

narration: Spread the same effort, and each visit lifts it.
Short visits, on later days.
Each one catches the fade.
The skill stays higher.
beats.visual_intent: On the second timeline the skill line gets a small lift at each thin slice and stays above the one-block line.

grounding.claim: Spread practice usually gives better long-term retention
Repeat attempts on later days with gaps

narration: Here is where people slip.
One big block feels like the serious option.
It is not the one that lasts.
For lasting, spread usually wins.
beats.visual_intent: The big block on the left labelled as feeling serious, next to the spread slices on the right labelled with the word usually.
beats.misconception: One focused block of practice is the best way to make it stick.

grounding.claim: Spread practice usually beats one block for lasting retention
Cramming feels productive

narration: That has a name. The spacing effect.
Same amount of practice, spread over sessions.
It usually lasts longer.
And we give no ideal gap.
beats.visual_intent: The name appears over the spread timeline, the two lines still visible, the spread one on top.

grounding.claim: The spacing effect: spread practice usually gives better retention than one block
No ideal gap claimed

narration: Remember where the icon dropped fastest?
Those early days are when a visit helps most.
Same effort. Spread it out.
beats.visual_intent: The first fading curve returns, its steep early stretch highlighted, a small visit marker placed in that stretch.

grounding.claim: Forgetting is fastest soon after learning
Spread practice usually lasts

narration: Back to Sam, a week on.
Sam decides to review.
Opens the recording.
Watches it again, start to finish.
Everything looks familiar.
beats.visual_intent: Sam watches the training recording on a screen, nodding, a thought bubble reading I know this.

grounding.claim: Sam re-watches the recording and it feels familiar
Re-watching feels familiar and easy

narration: Here is the tricky part.
Familiar is not the same as knowing.
Easy re-watching can fool you.
It feels like progress.
beats.visual_intent: Two labelled jars side by side next to Sam: one filled with a familiar glow, one empty labelled knowing.
beats.misconception: If I re-watch until it feels familiar and easy, I know it.

grounding.claim: Familiarity from re-watching can be mistaken for knowing

narration: So Sam closes the screen.
Opens the software, tries the task.
Blank. Not a single step comes.
Familiar, yes. Known, no.
beats.visual_intent: Sam shuts the recording, the software opens on an empty form, Sam's hands hover over the keys with nothing to type.

grounding.claim: Sam tries the task from memory and cannot start
Familiarity is mistaken for knowing

narration: Closed screen. Trying it from memory.
That has a name. Retrieval practice.
Do the task, or explain it,
without looking at anything.
beats.visual_intent: The name appears next to Sam's closed notes and open blank software, with the notes shown shut.

grounding.claim: Retrieval practice is recalling from memory without looking, such as doing the task from memory

narration: Then comes the part people skip.
Sam opens the recording, and checks.
Each miss goes on the notepad.
One step. Another. Another.
beats.visual_intent: Sam compares screen and recording; a gap list on the notepad fills in one missed step per phrase.

grounding.claim: Recall before checking, with feedback afterwards, helps
Sam lists the missed steps

narration: Why try first, then look?
Because the trying is what strengthens it.
Trying usually beats re-watching.
Looking afterwards fills the gaps.
beats.visual_intent: Two arrows on the notepad: try first, then check, in that order, with the gap list beside them.

grounding.claim: Recall usually strengthens memory more than re-watching, strongest before checking

narration: Now Sam feels bad.
Shaky, and some answers wrong.
Is that failure?
No. Somewhat hard is the working zone.
beats.visual_intent: Sam looks glum at a gap list with several entries; a speech bubble says this is not working, then a green zone band labelled somewhat hard appears around Sam's effort level.
beats.misconception: If my recall attempt is shaky or I get answers wrong, it is not working.

grounding.claim: Recall that feels somewhat hard, even with misses, tends to help more than effortless recall

narration: Effortless feels like progress.
Often it is not.
A few misses help more than none.
That has a name. Desirable difficulty.
beats.visual_intent: An easy-looking smooth path beside a slightly uphill path, with the name over the uphill one.

grounding.claim: Somewhat hard recall helps more; called desirable difficulty

narration: One limit. Keep it manageable.
An impossible task with no checking helps nobody.
Hard enough to stretch you.
Not so hard you quit.
beats.visual_intent: The uphill path with a sheer cliff drawn beyond it, crossed out, next to the manageable slope with a checkpoint flag.

grounding.claim: Difficulty must stay manageable; impossible tasks without feedback do not help

narration: Re-watching feels familiar.
Familiar is not knowing.
Try first, then check.
A few misses means it is working.
beats.visual_intent: Recap strip on the notepad: re-watch crossed out, try then check ticked, a few misses marked as normal.

grounding.claim: Familiarity is not knowing
Recall before check helps more than re-watching
Some misses are fine

narration: Now you.
Say Sam just finished a short training.
It covers a new approval tool.
Which plan lasts weeks later?
beats.visual_intent: Sam at the desk with a new approval tool on screen, three blank plan cards waiting on the side.

grounding.claim: Approval tool variation is an illustrative scene

narration: Plan A, re-watch the recording tonight.
Until it feels easy.
Plan B, try it tomorrow from memory,
check what you missed, repeat on a later day.
Plan C, one long block of practice today.
Pause, and decide.
on_screen: B. Try tomorrow, check, repeat later
beats.visual_intent: Three plan cards slide in one per option, each with a small picture: a screen, a notepad with a calendar, a single big block.

grounding.claim: Options are an illustrative decision in a fresh variation

narration: Plan B.
Plan A only feels like knowing.
Recall, then a check, spread over days, usually lasts.
beats.visual_intent: Card B lights up with a tick, card A dims with a tag familiar, not known; the other card fades away.

grounding.claim: Re-watching feels easy and the feeling is mistaken for knowing
Recall usually beats re-watching
Spread attempts on later days usually last

narration: So what does Sam do on the original task?
The one that went blank.
Three steps. Watch them.
beats.visual_intent: The blank form from the hook returns on Sam's screen, three empty step cards lined up beside it.

grounding.claim: Sam returns to the original task

narration: Step one. Close it, and try.
Sam shuts the notes and the recording.
Then does the task from memory.
Slowly. A few steps come.
beats.visual_intent: Card one fills in; the notes and recording shut, and Sam fills the form from memory, a few steps appearing.

grounding.claim: Close the material, try to do it from memory

narration: Step two. Check the misses.
Sam opens the recording, and compares.
Each missed step goes on the gap list.
That list is the next try's focus.
beats.visual_intent: Card two fills in; the gap list shows the missed steps, each one a line on the notepad.

grounding.claim: Then check what you missed

narration: Step three. Come back on a later day.
Same short try, with a gap between.
Not all at once.
beats.visual_intent: Card three fills in; a small calendar shows the try marked on a later day, with empty days between.

grounding.claim: Repeat the short recall attempt on later days with gaps

narration: Tie it to work that already happens.
Use the tool on a real task,
a few days after training.
No extra session to find.
on_screen: Use it on a real task
beats.visual_intent: On the calendar, the later-day marker is attached to a real task card in Sam's work week.

grounding.claim: Recall attempts can be tied to real work a few days after training

narration: Second try, a few days on.
Fewer misses.
Next one, fewer still.
Exact days matter less than having a spread.
beats.visual_intent: The gap list on the notepad shrinks across two later days, lines crossing off until only one remains.

grounding.claim: Any spaced schedule usually beats none; exact timing is not fixed
Sam's misses shrink over later tries

narration: That closed-book try?
Same as the better plan.
Close it, try it, check it.
on_screen: Close it, try it, check it
beats.visual_intent: Three step cards stacked side by side with the quiz card B beside them, matching their contents.

grounding.claim: Close, try from memory, check what was missed

narration: Now your week.
Think of your latest training.
What tool or skill came out of it?
Hold that one in mind.
beats.visual_intent: Split screen: Sam on the left, a blank week calendar on the right for the viewer.

grounding.claim: Viewer picks a tool or skill from their own recent training

narration: Pick one real task, a few days from now.
One that uses the skill anyway.
You are not adding work.
You are using work you have.
beats.visual_intent: On the blank calendar one day gets a task marker that uses the skill.

grounding.claim: Tie the recall attempt to work that already happens

narration: That is your later day.
Before you open any notes, try from memory.
Then check what you missed.
beats.visual_intent: A short try marker appears on the task day, a notes icon stays closed beside it, then a check mark follows.

grounding.claim: Try from memory first, then check what you missed
Do it a few days after training on a real task

narration: Here is the test.
Are you trying, or just looking?
Looking again is a re-read.
Trying first, then checking, is retrieval.
beats.visual_intent: Two calendar entries side by side: one an eye icon labelled re-read, the other a pencil over closed notes labelled retrieval.

grounding.claim: Re-reading feels familiar but is not the same as knowing
Recall without looking is retrieval practice

narration: Back to Sam, a week on.
Same desk, same software.
Sam starts the task, and misses one step.
Checks it, and carries on.
beats.visual_intent: The hook's desk scene returns with the same angle: Sam types through the task, pauses at one step, checks the notepad, continues; the skill icon is bright.

grounding.claim: Sam resolves the original situation

narration: Take this to work.
Close it, try it, check it,
and come back another day.
beats.visual_intent: Presenter beside four words appearing in turn, with Sam's bright icon on the desk behind.

grounding.claim: Close it, try from memory, check, repeat on later days
Repeat on later days
